label: input token a in the first four original positions (t<=3)
explanation: Fires only when the input token is the letter a during the original phase at steps 0-3 (99.9% of activation mass on in_tok=a; zero activation at t>=4, the delimiter, and essentially none in the copy phase, apart from 132 tiny copy-phase hits at t=5 plus rare weak hits on s/k). Every predicted step is active (precision 1.0). Magnitude depends on position and context: strongest at t=1, especially after i (i a reaches the max of 2.457), about 0.84 of max at t=0, and much weaker at t=3 (t=3 has a similar number of hits to t=0-2 but only 8% of the mass). A repeated a (one that already appeared earlier) gives a weaker activation (about 0.3-0.75 of max). Does not fire on a at later original positions, on a being output in the copy phase, or on other letters or digits.

issues: No systematic counterexample found. On the test split there are 0 false positives (precision 1.0). The 1269 missed active steps hold 0.1% of the mass. They are tiny hits on s or k at t=1 after i (about 0.02-0.03 of max) and copy-phase echoes of a (about 0.07-0.09). This is low-magnitude leakage, not a class the label misses.
Magnitude claims hold. t=1 has 34% of the mass (t=0: 30%, t=2: 27%), and t=3 has 22% of the active steps but only 8.2% of the mass. The top examples are all 'i a' at t=1 (1.00), and a at t=0 is 0.84.

Repeated-a claim holds with a small correction. With seen([tok('a')]) the predicate covers 4.6% of active steps and 3.7% of the mass. Examples show repeats at 0.25-0.75 of max, so the low end is about 0.25, not 0.3. Note that seen(['a']) with a string argument silently matches nothing, so seen() needs token indices.
Minor: 'i a' gets the max activation, but it is only 2.3% of the mass. The 'strongest at t=1' claim is driven by a at t=1 in general.
